1.q: לְ⁠דָוִ֨ד ׀ אַל־תִּתְחַ֥ר בַּ⁠מְּרֵעִ֑ים אַל־תְּ֝קַנֵּ֗א בְּ⁠עֹשֵׂ֥י עַוְלָֽה
1.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Do not let yourself be troubled by those who do evil] or [Do not be upset about evildoers; indeed, do not be envious of the doers of unrighteousness]

2.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the grass** quickly **withers** and dies, so the wicked will quickly perish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [just as the grass quickly withers, they will quickly perish]

The point of this comparison is that just as a **green plant** will **fade** and die, so the wicked will not last. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and just as a green plant fades, they too will fade away]

3.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **good**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the right thing]

The word translated as **feed** is used to describe what shepherds do for sheep as they care for them, and also for what sheep do as they feed themselves. So this could mean: (1) Cultivate, develop, or practice faithfulness to Yahweh (and each other). Alternate translation: [and practice faithfulness] or (2) Enjoy the faithfulness that Yahweh offers to his people. Alternate translation: [and experience Yahweh’s faithfulness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and act faithfully]

4.note: Here the **heart** represents where a person’s **desires** exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what you truly desire]

5.note: David is using **Roll your way upon Yahweh** as a common expression of his culture to mean to turn over or entrust your plans to Yahweh. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Commit your plans to Yahweh]

David is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he will act** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Yahweh is the only one who can do this. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh himself will act]

6.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **the light** is clearly visible to everyone, so Yahweh will make the person’s righteousness clearly evident. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [your righteousness so that it is as clearly visible as the light]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how righteous you are]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and publicly defend your just cause]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the noonday** sun shines at its brightest, so Yahweh will make the person’s justice unmistakably clear. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and he will bring out that you are innocent so that it is as clear as the noonday sun]

7.note: David is using **Be silent to Yahweh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “wait patiently and reverently for Yahweh.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Rest quietly before Yahweh]

The word translated as **tremble** represents the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense here. Scholars have proposed that a different word with a similar spelling was intended that means “to wait” that seems to better fit the meaning of this passage. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [and wait]
The pronoun **him** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and tremble for Yahweh]

David is speaking of how a wicked person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a wicked person’s way]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **schemes**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [carrying out wicked plans]

8.note: The terms **nose** and **wrath** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [of intense anger]

David is using the **nose** here as a common expression of the culture, **the burning of his nose** to mean “anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [of anger]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wrath**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [being furious]

9.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Since]

David is using **cut off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “destroy.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [evildoers will perish]

The expression **will be cut off** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will cut off evildoers]

David is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they will inherit** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that, unlike the evildoers in the previous line, those who wait for Yahweh will inherit the land. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [they themselves will inherit the land]

10.note: David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And yet a little while and then there are no more]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked person]
The pronoun **his** refers to the wicked person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [where the wicked person was]

11.note: David is using the adjective **meek** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [But meek people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [living so peacefully and prosperously]

12.note: David is using the adjectives **wicked** and **righteous** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [The wicked person is plotting against the righteous person]

The pronoun **his** refers to the wicked person, while the pronoun **him** refers to the righteous person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the wicked person is gnashing his teeth against the righteous person]

The action of **gnashing his teeth** describes a symbolic action by which the wicked person expresses rage and contempt against the righteous person. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and showing his rage against the righteous]

13.note: David is speaking of **the Lord** as if he were a person who could **laugh at** someone. This represents the Lord’s contempt for the wicked person and his plans. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The Lord regards him with contempt]

The pronoun **he** refers to the Lord, while the pronoun **his** refers to the wicked person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Lord sees that the wicked person’s day is coming]

David is speaking of the wicked person’s judgment as if it were a time or a **day** that is **coming** toward him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the time of his judgment is near]

14.note: David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Those who are wicked]

Here, **to** marks **bring down the poor and the needy** as the goal or purpose of the wicked preparing their weapons to kill, having **opened a sword** and **trodden their bow**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. [in order to bring down the poor and the needy]

David is using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [those who are poor people and needy]

The terms **the poor** and **the needy** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the very vulnerable]

David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who live uprightly]

15.note: David is speaking as if the violent plans of the wicked were a **sword** that would pierce their own **heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Their own schemes will bring about their ruin]

The expression **will be broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will destroy their bows]

16.note: David is using the possessive form to describe the **little** amount that **the righteous** person possesses as being far better in contrast to the great wealth or **abundance** that **many wicked** people possess. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Better is what little the righteous person owns than what many wicked people have in abundance]

17.note: David is speaking as if the strength of the wicked were **arms** that could be **broken**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the power of the wicked will fail]

The expression **will be broken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will break the arms of the wicked]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked]

Here David is speaking of Yahweh’s care and protection as if he were physically holding up or **supporting** the righteous. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but Yahweh protects and sustains the righteous]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are righteous]

18.note: David is using **knowing the days of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “concerned for the needs of.” This refers to Yahweh’s intimate and active involvement in the life of his people. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is concerned for the needs of]

David is using the possessive form to describe the **days** that **the blameless** live. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the days that the blameless live]

David is using the adjective **blameless** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who live blameless lives]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and what they inherit]

19.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the blameless people from the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The blameless will not have shame]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [They will not be ashamed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a time when evil things happen]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **famine**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and in the days when people are starving]

20.note: David uses the word **For** here to indicate a contrast between the fate of “the blameless” mentioned in vs. 18 and the fate of **the wicked**. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [However,]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked]

The word translated as **pastures** could also be translated as “rams.” So this could refer to: (1) flowers that grow in the meadows and then quickly fade away. Alternate translation: [will be like the flowers of the meadow] or (2) the choicest parts of the ram that is offered for sacrifice. Alternate translation: [will be like the choice parts of rams]

The point of this comparison is that just as the wildflower in the field or **the precious of pastures** is beautiful but quickly fades away, so **the enemies of Yahweh** will quickly perish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and the enemies of Yahweh will be like flowers in the meadow that quickly wither]

David is using the adjective **precious** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [will be like the beautiful flowers in the pastures]

David is speaking of the disappearance of the wicked as if they were **smoke** that quickly vanishes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they disappear completely, they are utterly gone]

21.note: David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [The wicked person]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [but the righteous person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **grace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is acting graciously]

22.note: The pronoun **him** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [those blessed by Yahweh]

The expression **will be cut off** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [but Yahweh will cut off those he has cursed]

David is using **be cut off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “be destroyed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will be destroyed]

23.note: The expression **are established** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh establishes people’s steps]

David is speaking of a person’s life course as if it were **steps** that a person walks. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the life of a man is directed]

David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [each person]

David is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he delights in the way he lives]
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh, while the pronoun **his** refers to the man. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh delights in that man’s way]

24.note: David is presenting a possible condition, that a righteous man might have something bad happen to him. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [Even if he falls]
The pronoun **he**and **his** in this verse refer to the righteous man described in verse 23. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the righteous man falls]

Here David is speaking of the reaction the righteous have to difficult times as if he stumbles and **falls**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he has difficult times]

The expression **will not be hurled down** contains a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [nothing will hurl him down]

David is speaking of Yahweh’s help as if Yahweh were physically holding him up by **supporting his hand**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is helping him]

25.note: The word **abandoned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh abandoning the righteous]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [any righteous person]

Here David is speaking of the offspring of the righteous person as if they were actually his **seed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [or his offspring]
David is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for enough food to eat]

26.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the righteous person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the righteous person is showing grace]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **grace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he is being gracious]

Here David is speaking of the offspring of the righteous person as if they were actually his **seed**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his offspring]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **blessing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [are able to bless others]

27.note: David is speaking of **evil** as if it were an object that they should physically **turn away** from. Your language may have a comparable expression you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Stop doing what is bad]

If your language does not use an abstract nouns for the ideas of **evil** and **good**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [from doing evil things and instead do good things]

28.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is just]

David is using the adjective **faithful** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [his faithful people]

The expression **are preserved** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh preserves them]

The expression **will be cut off** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [but Yahweh will cut off the offspring of the wicked]

David is using the possessive form to describe **offspring** that belong to **the wicked**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [but the children of wicked people]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked]

David is using **be cut off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “be destroyed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will be destroyed]

29.note: David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Righteous people]

30.note: David is using one part of a person, his **mouth**, to mean all of him in the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The righteous person]

David is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the righteous person]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wisdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [wise words]

David is using one part of a person, his **tongue**, to mean all of the righteous person in the act of speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he speaks justice]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what is just]

31.note: David is using the possessive form to describe a **law** that comes from **his God**. Also, by using the phrase **his God** he does not mean that the righteous person possesses or controls Yahweh, but rather to emphasize that Yahweh is the God he worships. See the introduction to Psalms for further discussion. Alternate translation: [The law given by the God whom he worships]

Here the **his heart** represents where a person’s thoughts exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is always in his thoughts]

David is speaking as if the righteous person were walking along a path and his **steps** could **slip**. He means that the righteous person will not fail in his conduct. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he will not fail in the way he lives]

32.note: David is using the adjectives **wicked** and **righteous** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [The wicked person is watching the righteous person]
The pronoun **him** refers to the righteous person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to kill the righteous person]

33.q: יְ֭הוָה לֹא־יַעַזְבֶ֣⁠נּוּ בְ⁠יָד֑⁠וֹ וְ⁠לֹ֥א יַ֝רְשִׁיעֶ֗⁠נּוּ בְּ⁠הִשָּׁפְטֽ⁠וֹ
33.note: In this verse, both of uses of the pronoun **him** refer to the righteous person as well as the **he** at the end while the pronoun **his** refers to the wicked person. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will not abandon the righteous person into the hand of the wicked person, and will not condemn the righteous person when he is judged]

Here, **his hand** represents the power of the wicked person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the power of the wicked person]

The expression **is judged** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [when he comes to trial]

34.note: David is speaking of how Yahweh wants a person to live as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and live how he wants you to live]

David is using the possessive form to describe a **way** that belongs to **Yahweh**. He means the way of living that Yahweh prescribes. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way that Yahweh commands]

Here David is speaking of honoring someone as if they were and object that someone would **raise** up. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will honor you in order for you]

David is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [When those who are wicked are cut off]

The expression **are cut off** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh cuts off the wicked]

David is using **cut off** as a common expression of the culture to mean “destroyed.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [When the wicked are destroyed]

35.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a green native tree** spreads out and flourishes, so the wicked person was **spreading himself out** and becoming powerful. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [becoming powerful like a flourishing native tree that spreads out]

36.note: The pronouns **he** and **him** throughout this verse refer to the wicked person mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the wicked man passed away]

The expression **was not found** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but I could not find him]

37.note: The psalmist is using the adjectives **blameless** and **upright** as nouns to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [blameless people and see upright people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **future**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [there is something good ahead]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **man** that is characterized by **peace**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the peaceful man]

David is not referring to a specific **man**. He means anyone in general who lives peacefully. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [for anyone who lives peacefully]

38.note: The expression **are destroyed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language.
